title: Compliance readiness — choose your path
summary: A public, no-PII learning graph for understanding controls, evidence, remediation, and independent-review boundaries.

nodes.title: What brought you here?
nodes.prompt: Choose the situation closest to your job today. You can loop back and take another path at any time.
learningObjectives: Separate readiness work from an independent assurance decision.
Choose a path based on the work you need to understand, not a framework acronym alone.

checkpoints.label: I understand this public training does not collect evidence or make an audit determination.
I understand Canonical Plus prepares readiness work while qualified independent parties make formal determinations.

choices.label: A buyer asked whether we are compliant
choices.summary: Start with scope, commitments, and the buyer request.

choices.label: I need to turn a gap into engineering work
choices.summary: Start from a system change and work backward to control intent.

choices.label: I own security or compliance controls
choices.summary: Start with control design and proof.

choices.label: I keep rebuilding evidence for every review

nodes.title: Translate the buyer request into a readiness scope
nodes.prompt: A request such as “Are you SOC 2 compliant?” is not yet a project plan. Identify the product, environments, data, entities, time horizon, and the independent artifact the buyer actually expects.
learningObjectives: Turn a broad compliance question into an explicit system and framework scope.
Distinguish a readiness estimate from a completed independent report or certification.

checkpoints.label: I would define the in-scope system before promising an outcome or date.
I would identify which independent party, if any, must issue the final report, certification, or authorization.

choices.label: Map the request to frameworks and shared controls
Understand what evidence the buyer or assessor will need

nodes.title: A finding becomes an engineering change
nodes.prompt: Suppose the gap is weak production access. The readiness task is not “be compliant”; it is a bounded change such as stronger identity, least privilege, approval, logging, review, and evidence of operation.
learningObjectives: Translate a compliance gap into technical acceptance criteria.
Keep the control objective distinct from one specific implementation.

checkpoints.label: I can describe the desired security outcome and how we will prove it operates.
I understand a framework control rarely mandates one vendor or code pattern.

choices.label: Design the control before implementing it
What if we cannot finish the change before review?

nodes.title: A control needs an owner, trigger, action, and proof
nodes.prompt: A useful control explains who performs it, when it runs, what system or population it covers, how exceptions are handled, and what durable evidence shows it operated.
learningObjectives: Recognize operational control components beyond policy text.
Design evidence as part of the control instead of after the fact.

checkpoints.label: I can name an owner and trigger for the control.
I can name the system-generated or review evidence the control should leave behind.

choices.label: Turn that proof into an evidence operation
See how one control maps to multiple frameworks

nodes.title: Frameworks overlap; implementations should not multiply blindly
nodes.prompt: Access control, change management, incident handling, vendor risk, backups, and logging often satisfy multiple obligations. Map one real control to many requirements rather than creating a separate process for every framework row.
learningObjectives: Use common-control mapping to reduce duplicate work.
Preserve framework-specific qualifiers even when implementation is shared.

checkpoints.label: I would reuse a real control across frameworks when the control objective truly overlaps.
I would still record framework-specific scope, evidence, or assessor expectations.

choices.label: Classify what is actually missing

nodes.title: Evidence is an operating system, not a screenshot scramble
nodes.prompt: Good evidence has an owner, source, population, period, freshness rule, retention rule, and a way to explain exceptions. Prefer durable system records over one-off screenshots when the system can produce better proof.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a control from evidence that the control operated.
Define evidence freshness, provenance, and retention deliberately.

checkpoints.label: I can identify the authoritative source for at least one important control.
I can explain when that evidence becomes stale or incomplete.

choices.label: Distinguish missing control from missing proof
Learn how incidents and exceptions affect evidence

nodes.title: Classify the gap before assigning remediation
nodes.prompt: A finding can mean the control does not exist, exists but is badly designed, exists but did not operate, operated but lacks proof, or is out of scope because the boundary was wrong. Those are different problems.
learningObjectives: Classify findings before prescribing fixes.
Avoid engineering work that only papers over an evidence problem.

checkpoints.label: I can distinguish a control-design gap from an evidence gap.
I would re-check scope before treating every observation as a remediation task.

choices.label: Build the remediation sequence

nodes.title: Exceptions should be explicit, bounded, and reviewable
nodes.prompt: A missed control or security incident does not disappear because a review date is close. Record the fact, owner, risk, compensating measures, remediation date, and evidence. Independent reviewers decide how that history affects their conclusion.
learningObjectives: Treat exceptions as governed records instead of hidden failures.
Keep compensating controls and remediation evidence explicit.

checkpoints.label: I would not delete or conceal an exception to make a readiness score look better.
I would record owner, risk, compensating measures, and a remediation target.

choices.label: Move the exception into a remediation plan
Revisit durable evidence operations

nodes.title: Prioritize by risk, dependency, and proof
nodes.prompt: A useful roadmap names the gap, desired state, owner, dependencies, acceptance criteria, evidence, due date, and rollback or exception path. Sequence identity, logging, change control, data, and infrastructure work so later controls can rely on earlier ones.
learningObjectives: Turn observations into reviewable engineering and operating tasks.
Sequence work by dependency rather than checklist order alone.

checkpoints.label: Every remediation item I create will have an owner and evidence expectation.
I will order dependent controls instead of treating every row as independent work.

choices.label: Prepare for independent review

nodes.title: Know where readiness stops
nodes.prompt: Canonical Plus can help organize scope, controls, evidence, remediation, and open questions. The independent auditor, assessor, certification body, regulator, or legal adviser applies the formal criteria and issues any conclusion within their authority.
learningObjectives: Preserve independence between preparation and formal determination.
Hand over evidence with assumptions and exceptions intact.

checkpoints.label: I will not describe a readiness score as an audit opinion, certification, or authorization.
I will include unresolved assumptions and exceptions in the handoff rather than hiding them.

choices.label: Finish this training path
Loop back and practice framework mapping again

nodes.title: Choose the operating model that fits your next step
nodes.prompt: You now have the core readiness model. Pick the kind of help that best matches the work in front of your team; this is a learning recommendation, not a binding quote.
learningObjectives: Connect readiness work to an appropriate operating cadence.
Keep commercial scope subordinate to a reviewed statement of work.

checkpoints.label: I understand package selection does not change the independent-review boundary.
I understand actual scope and price are controlled by a signed SOW.

choices.label: We need a scoped baseline and remediation roadmap
We need recurring evidence and readiness operations
We need hands-on technical remediation and automation

nodes.title: Your next learning path: Foundation Readiness
nodes.prompt: A baseline is useful when the main uncertainty is scope, gap classification, ownership, and remediation order.
learningObjectives: Know when a baseline readiness engagement is sufficient before moving into recurring operations.

checkpoints.label: I understand this recommendation is educational and the public price is a proposed starting assumption.

choices.label: Choose another adventure
Practice framework mapping

outcome.message: Start with scope, a gap register, and an executable remediation roadmap.

nodes.title: Your next learning path: Managed Readiness
nodes.prompt: Recurring operations are useful when evidence freshness, control ownership, exceptions, and review preparation need an operating cadence.
learningObjectives: Know when continuous evidence and control-owner routines matter more than another one-time checklist.

checkpoints.label: I understand this recommendation is educational and the public price is a proposed starting assumption.

choices.label: Choose another adventure
Practice evidence operations

outcome.message: Operate controls, evidence freshness, exceptions, and handoff preparation continuously.

nodes.title: Your next learning path: Assurance Engineering
nodes.prompt: Hands-on assurance engineering is useful when the blockers are materially technical and the team needs help implementing or automating the remediation itself.
learningObjectives: Know when readiness work should include direct engineering remediation support.

checkpoints.label: I understand assurance engineering still does not make Canonical Plus the independent auditor or certification body.

choices.label: Choose another adventure
Practice an engineering finding again

outcome.message: Pair readiness leadership with hands-on remediation and evidence automation.
